entries.name: Maximum pseudolikelihood estimation
entries.definition: A parameter-estimation method that maximizes the product of a specified model’s sitewise full conditional probabilities or densities evaluated at the observed configuration.
entries.identity_notes: The classical full-conditional pseudolikelihood uses every observed site. It is an estimation objective and does not specify a unique numerical optimizer. It is distinct from full joint maximum likelihood, independent-site coding likelihood, iterative conditional modes for state optimization, and iterative conditional estimation for incomplete-data parameters. A general loss assembled from unrelated conditionals is not automatically the pseudolikelihood of a compatible joint model. The paper discusses fixed-site spatial models without assuming stationarity or homogeneity; the local graph and parameterization must still be specified. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, yielding 35 and 35 matched lines; all 23 unique contents were read. Hits are citations, contextual statements and discovery leads rather than records of these identities. All 182 semantic label/synonym hits were read. Thirty-one fully annotated exact CLASS nodes and outgoing edges were inspected: 23 byte-equivalent to prior inspected nodes and eight freshly read. Short acronyms were included in the normalized identity comparison. Absence is bounded to the pinned snapshot, maintained corpus and inspected semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The product of normalized full conditionals is generally not a normalized joint distribution over x. Its maximizer need not equal the joint-likelihood maximizer. Dividing that product by a parameter-dependent joint normalizer changes the objective.

Conditionals must be compatible with the intended joint model and parameters must lie in its valid domain. Optimizing local expressions without these restrictions can produce inadmissible joint parameters. Gaussian variance positivity and precision positive definiteness remain necessary.

The source gives a consistency sketch for an infinite bounded-degree site system with growing coding classes and additional regularity and boundary conditions. It is not a universal theorem for arbitrary growing graphs, fixed finite samples, misspecified models or every parameterization.

Efficiency, uncertainty estimates and likelihood-ratio calibration do not automatically follow ordinary independent-sample likelihood formulas. Strong dependence, limited information, boundaries and model mismatch require separate assessment; the source offers no universal efficiency advantage.

Gaussian least-squares expressions apply to the stated common-variance and compatible symmetric interaction parameterization. Design inverses, ratio denominators, finite maximizers and nonzero residual variance require checks. Alternating algebraic updates are not a proof of a global optimum.

A partition into coding sets does not make the corresponding estimators or test statistics independent. The pseudolikelihood maximizer is not generally the arithmetic mean of coding-set maximizers. Original finite objective comparisons demonstrate this distinction; no empirical fitting, author code or benchmark was run.

claims.statement: For an observed configuration x and a compatible family p_theta with well-defined full conditionals, form PL(theta;x)=product_i p_theta(x_i|x_(-i)) and maximize sum_i log p_theta(x_i|x_(-i)) over the admissible parameter space. In a Markov field, each factor depends only on the site’s neighbors; a global joint partition function cancels from that factor, although its local normalizer still must be evaluated. If the sites are partitioned into nonneighbor coding sets, the log pseudolikelihood is the sum of their conditional log likelihoods. This identity combines objectives, not the separately fitted parameter values. For the source’s proper common-conditional-variance Gaussian model with mean D*a, symmetric B=I-phi*H and variance sigma^2, the residual term is (x-D*a)^T B^2(x-D*a)/sigma^2. Its joint Gaussian likelihood instead includes log|B| and a single-B quadratic. Complete independence is a special case in which the product of full conditionals equals the joint likelihood.

entries.name: Maximum coding likelihood estimation
entries.definition: A conditional parameter-estimation method that selects mutually non-neighboring sites in a Markov field and maximizes their joint conditional likelihood, which factors into sitewise full conditionals given the remaining observed sites.
entries.identity_notes: This record uses the classical independent-site coding method of Besag. Coding selects a graph-independent subset; it does not encode features, compress data or learn sparse representations. Shifted or alternative coding sets can give additional dependent estimates. Extensions using conditionally dependent blocks require their joint conditional likelihoods rather than this independent-singleton product. The method is distinct from multiplying all site conditionals as pseudolikelihood and from state updates in ICM or Gibbs sampling. limitations: The factorization needs a valid graph and the stated joint conditional-independence property. It is not justified by spatial distance alone or by arbitrary, incompatible local distributions. Hard support constraints require separate treatment beyond the positive-model construction.

Choosing a large independent set need not yield a unique selection or the most informative estimator. Conditioning omits some likelihood information while retaining the complement as covariates; it does not literally discard all white-site observations.

Estimates and tests from shifted coding patterns reuse the same configuration and are generally dependent. Combining them requires a justified procedure; neither naive independent-test calibration nor an arithmetic average of estimates is automatically optimal.

Conditional likelihood-ratio comparisons require comparable selected dependent sites and conditioning sets. The source warns against comparing fits based on different codings as if they were the same likelihood. Ordinary asymptotic approximations still require identifiability, information and regularity conditions.

The source’s unconstrained coding estimates can violate the intended joint-model parameter restrictions. A conditional objective may be finite where the full Gaussian field is invalid, so the parameter domain must be enforced. Averaging happened to yield admissible values in some reported examples and is not a general repair.

The inspected plant and wheat data illustrate estimation and model diagnostics, while exposing model inadequacy and aggregation effects. They do not prove general efficiency or spatial prediction accuracy. No empirical data fitting, author implementation or benchmark was reproduced.

claims.statement: For a compatible positive Markov-field model with observed configuration x, choose a nonempty set S containing no neighboring pair and let C be its complement. Conditional on X_C=x_C, the variables in S are mutually independent, so L_S(theta;x_S|x_C)=product_(i in S) p_theta(x_i|x_(-i)). Maximize its log over valid theta. The complement supplies conditioning values even though its own site likelihood factors are omitted. A rectangular four-neighbor graph admits checkerboard coding; adding diagonal interactions requires another independent-set design, such as the source’s four shifted patterns. Changing the selected set changes the conditional likelihood. The full-site pseudolikelihood equals the product of coding likelihoods for a partition into independent sets, but maximizing that product differs in general from averaging separately fitted parameters.

entries.name: Auto-normal Markov random field
entries.definition: A proper finite Gaussian Markov-field model specified by linear full-conditional means and positive, value-independent site conditional variances, with compatibility enforced by a symmetric positive-definite joint precision matrix.
entries.identity_notes: The record is scoped to the proper finite auto-normal construction. It is a Gaussian conditional-autoregressive representation of a multivariate normal law with a specified conditional-dependence graph. Intrinsic improper Gaussian fields and infinite-lattice extensions require separate existence or constraint conditions and are not exact aliases here. Spatial conditional autoregression is not temporal autoregression and is not the simultaneous autoregressive model obtained by treating the same local residual equations as independent noise equations. Gaussian-process regression conditions a process prior on training observations for prediction; this record specifies the finite graphical joint law itself. It can be used as a prior but does not inherently introduce hidden labels or independent observation emissions. limitations: Every site conditional can be individually normalized while the proposed collection fails to define a proper joint law. Weighted symmetry and positive definiteness must both hold. With unequal conditional variances, raw beta coefficients need not be symmetric.

A singular precision can describe an intrinsic improper construction only with additional interpretation or constraints; it is not the ordinary normalized Gaussian density stated here. An indefinite precision gives a nonintegrable quadratic model. Positive diagonal entries alone are insufficient.

Finite-graph eigenvalue bounds depend on the actual graph and boundary conditions. Infinite-lattice stationarity criteria are not automatically necessary finite-graph conditions. The source’s stationary or homogeneous examples do not require every finite auto-normal model to share those assumptions.
Missing precision edges encode conditional independence, not marginal independence or causal effects. A sparse simultaneous-equation matrix can induce additional precision edges.

Unconstrained conditional least-squares, coding-likelihood or pseudolikelihood estimates may leave the proper joint parameter domain. The Gaussian fitting objective and parameter identifiability depend on the specified mean, graph and interaction parameterization; existence of a covariance representation does not ensure identifiable scientific parameters.

The source’s wheat and plant examples expose aggregation, nonstationarity and model-fit concerns; a fitted Gaussian field does not establish a causal spatial mechanism or universal predictive adequacy. The record does not certify source implementations, empirical fits or infinite-system convergence.

claims.statement: For site i, specify X_i given all other sites as normal with mean mu_i+sum_(j!=i) beta_ij*(x_j-mu_j) and variance v_i>0 independent of the conditioning values. Let B have diagonal 1 and off-diagonal -beta_ij, and let Lambda=diag(v_i). These conditionals define the proper finite joint model when Q=Lambda^(-1)*B is symmetric positive definite. Symmetry requires beta_ij*v_j=beta_ji*v_i. The joint law is N(mu,Q^(-1)), with density proportional to |Q|^(1/2)*exp[-(x-mu)^T Q(x-mu)/2]. A zero off-diagonal precision entry denotes conditional independence given the other sites; marginal covariance need not vanish. With common v_i=sigma^2, compatibility reduces to symmetric positive-definite B and covariance sigma^2*B^(-1). In contrast, the simultaneous equations B*(X-mu)=epsilon with independent epsilon~N(0,Lambda) imply covariance B^(-1)*Lambda*B^(-T) and precision B^T*Lambda^(-1)*B. For the proper conditional model, a factorization Q=C^T*C allows exact Gaussian sampling as mu+C^(-1)*z with independent standard-normal z.

mapping_assessment: MPLE and independent-site coding likelihood map related to ProbabilisticGraphicalModel for parameter estimation using compatible graph conditionals; the pinned class is task-scoped, not an algorithm superclass. The proper finite auto-normal family maps broad to Model and related to ProbabilisticGraphicalModel. MachineLearningTask is more generic and does not distinguish the objectives. TrainingStrategy is preprocessing-scoped; supervised or unsupervised contexts are not imposed as intrinsic identities. SpatialRegression, RegressionAnalysis, GeneralizedLinearModel, LinearRegression and LogisticRegression describe regression tasks or model contexts, not these particular estimation objectives or every Gaussian joint field. A local regression formula does not equate a compatible joint spatial law with an exogenous regression task. MarkovChain, AutoregressiveMovingAverage and VectorAutoregression require temporal/sequential structure absent from a general spatial graph. BayesianNetwork and CausalGraphicalModel do not preserve the same undirected graph by arbitrary factorization or imply causal interventions. AutoregressiveLanguageModel, EnergyBasedLLM and ImplicitLanguageModel are language-scoped. AutoEncoderNetwork, DenoisingAutoEncoder, SparseAutoEncoder and VariationalAutoEncoder denote neural architectures rather than auto-normal fields. SparseLearning refers to sparse dictionary representations, and CategoryEncodingLayer to feature encoding; neither is graph-independent-set coding likelihood. Normalization changes data scale rather than certifying a joint probability normalizer. GaussianNoiseLayer, GaussianDropoutLayer, HiddenLayer and ProbabilisticHiddenLayer are neural components. MaximumLayer is an elementwise tensor operation, not likelihood optimization. Native MRF, HMRF, HMT, EM, ICE, ICM, Gibbs sampling and Gaussian-process regression distinguish joint field, latent/observed partition, topology, parameter estimation, state optimization, sampling and predictive process conditioning. Contextual reading does not renew their scientific approval.

notes: PDF pp.1–2 visually read: JSTOR wrapper and printed p.179 abstract/introduction. Julian Besag, Statistical Analysis of Non-lattice Data, The Statistician24(3):179–195,September1975. Printed page=PDF page+177. Fixed irregularly located sites carry continuous/discrete dependent variables; objectives are model specification, parameter estimation and goodness of fit. Abstract promises three methods, the last Gaussian-specific, with reservations about practical investigation. Wheat residual spatial correlation is motivating context, not proof of method performance. Full methods remain unread.

PDF pp.3–6 / printed180–183: spatial neighbor relations encode conditional dependence, not causal intervention. Compatible full conditionals require restrictions; the brief Hammersley–Clifford summary is qualified by the original theorem assumptions, not a blanket result for all support constraints. Section2.2 gives conditional Gaussian means mu_i+sum_j beta_ij(x_j-mu_j), constant positive conditional variances sigma_i^2, B diagonal1/offdiagonal−beta, Lambda=diag(sigma_i^2). Joint covariance is B^-1 Lambda and precision Lambda^-1 B must be symmetric positive definite, so beta_ij*sigma_j^2=beta_ji*sigma_i^2. Every proper finite multivariate Gaussian admits this conditional representation; sparsity adds the selected graph restriction. Section2.3 simultaneous autoregression uses covariance B^-1 Lambda B^-T with invertible B; using the same coefficients in conditional and simultaneous constructions is not generally equivalent, and SAR may be nonidentified. Remaining PDF pp.7–18 unread.

PDF pp.7–10 / printed184–187: SAR residuals are correlated with other observations, so conditioning the simultaneous equation cannot simply set conditional residual expectation to zero. Sparse four-neighbor SAR creates larger conditional neighborhoods (diagonal and distance-two terms). The paper distinguishes conditional from marginal independence. Sections2.4–2.5 discuss mean regression mu=D theta, selecting graph/weights, and compatibility of boundary-length weights: beta_ij=(l_ij/l_i)*d_ij^(-kappa)*phi requires conditional variance sigma^2/l_i, not common variance, on a connected system. Symmetry alone still needs positive definiteness. Rescaling by sqrt(l_i) also transforms coefficients and means. Parameterization suggestions are not empirical validation. Gaussian SAR simulation x=mu+B^-1 Lambda^(1/2)e has the stated covariance; conditional Gaussian simulation continues on the next page. Remaining pp.11–18 unread.

PDF pp.11–14 / printed188–191: auto-normal simulation factors precision Q=C^T C and uses x=mu+C^-1 e. Section3.2 coding chooses a nonneighbor independent set S and maximizes sum_(i in S) log p_i(x_i|x_-i,psi), the true likelihood of selected black sites conditional on fixed white complement under a compatible graph model. White values still enter as conditioning data; only their own likelihood factors are omitted. Choice of large coding set is nonunique; asymptotic conditional likelihood theory needs regularity/information conditions, not merely many selected sites. Section3.3 pseudolikelihood sums all site log conditionals, generally not joint log likelihood. Source explicitly lacked established sampling properties at that point and gives no universal efficiency guarantee. For common-variance Gaussian conditionals, beta=phi H and mu=D theta, symmetric H, PL reduces to residual SSE (x-Dtheta)^T B^2(x-Dtheta), B=I-phi H; inverse/ratio updates in Equations3.5–3.7 require identifiability, nonzero denominators, positive variance and valid positive-definite B. Unconstrained algebraic updates need not remain admissible. SAR residual correlations invalidate a naive zero conditional residual argument; the next page continues the consistency comparison. Remaining pp.15–18 unread.

PDF pp.15–18 / printed192–195 complete the paper and all references. Section3.3 sketches consistency using an infinite bounded-degree site system, finitely many nonneighbor color classes whose sizes grow, consistency of coding estimators and additional unspecified regularity/boundary conditions. This is not a universal proof for fixed finite graphs, arbitrary growing graphs or parameterizations; zero expected score alone is insufficient. Pseudolikelihood log objective is the sum of coding-class log objectives, not generally an arithmetic average of their maximizers. Equal expectations of residual quadratics do not make the finite-data objectives/estimators equal. Final remarks call for practical validation and explicitly correct an earlier isolated claim about spatial-temporal models: continuous-time evolution can induce within-time dependence after temporal subsampling.
